Pooja Ranjan: Thank you. Welcome to EIPIP Meeting Number 132. Today is November 18th, and the agenda is added on Ethereum slash PM. GitHub issue, the number is 2288. On agenda, we have AI in EIP ecosystem, some discussions, some presentations. And some editors point to figure out on how we can make the EIP process even more beneficial for the ecosystem so we can move forward faster. So we have listed some exceptional PR merging circumstances. We'll discuss on that. Further, we have called for input and updates from previous meetings. We are joined by Jochem, so I would like to invite him to maybe kick off this meeting with AI in the EIP ecosystem. He has agents.md to be shared. Jochem?
jochem-brouwer: Yes, can you see my screen?
Pooja Ranjan: Yes.

jochem-brouwer: I want to quote EIP-5069, which says it is imperative that the EIP process evolves, albeit cautiously. So, what AI also changes is that we see the EIP and the ERC influx, which is much higher. At least that's my perception. And what's also changing is that these documents are much more complex than we have seen in the past. So, what I used to do in the past is, at my lunch break, I would grab a coffee and then read an EIP, especially on the EL side. It is not possible anymore at all at this point, because these EIPs are incredibly complex. So the logical next step, I think, is to automate reviews using AI. And then the question is, what are we actually going to automate? Because we can now address stuff which we could not address automatically before.

jochem-brouwer: What AI can address that was not possible in the past: things like backward references, so if you reference something backward, that things are first defined. And then that abbreviations, if you are using them, that they are defined. That documents are self-contained. That it has the correct copyright. And the claims in the documents, that we can actually use AI to verify these claims. So this is a nice property of AI. We should be careful, because we should not use too much AI. Because most of the EIPs or ERCs are, at some point, written by AI. And the problem is if people then use AI's feedback loop, the problem is if people use AI to then address a review, then you create a feedback loop where the ecosystem is basically a forum which only AI agents reply to. So this is something I think is very bad: if you have an original idea, and you use AI to generate it, and then we have a feedback loop reviewed by AI, and this review moves the original idea away. So I think the fix for this is that AI does not propose the changes, but rather asks questions to the author.

jochem-brouwer: Uh, with some small exceptions, like if an abbreviation is first defined, then you can directly suggest, okay, you likely meant this, so maybe apply just a suggestion. And… Yeah, let me see if I can say anything else about this. Uh… Yeah, so the main idea here is that AI does not move the original idea from the original idea what the author had in mind. So again, we should use AI, I think, but not too much. And again, EIP-5069, it's imperative that the EIP process evolves, albeit cautiously. So the main thing: automerge is something I think we should absolutely not do. And so what is AI review for? So we do not have to read the entire EIP. And this is the question: what do we guard in this process? So on the EIP site, we guard that the entry point is high-level ideas of improvements to the Ethereum protocol.

jochem-brouwer: What is also of course guarded is the EIP or ERC number, which are doing so if someone references to your EIP or ERC number. It is very clear what we are talking about, and another nice property of the EIPs or the ERCs is that it is a memory for the ecosystem, to figure out why we are actually proposing this kind of changes. And of course, if you have a new idea, then the entry point for the EIP process to propose your idea is an EIP. And as editor, we of course do not make any decisions. So we stay neutral on this, even if in our personal opinion it does not make any sense, then this is not our task as editor. We will just move forward so people can discuss on ACD, because that's for ACD, and that's not our job. So who then changes or merges the changes on the site? So these AI reviews are automated, and I want to start a pilot with this. The current reviews, what I'm doing, is a hybrid mode. So it is, I open the EIP, and I point an agent to it, with access only to open the EIP's repository. And then what it does is close pending review to get updated. And then I check all these comments, do they make sense or do they not make sense? Because I don't want to bring any false positives or tasks that give extra work to the author. I want this automated process to be in a private kind of mind, but I want to publish the reviews. This is read-only. So if it approves or whatever, that this will not move the EIP forward. But our responsibility is that we answer that it is not total slop, it is not a total scam. Because we have to realize, of course, EIPs, these documents are also open to abuse. So we should be very careful about this. And therefore, this is also part of responsibility: we should look at an EIP, let's say to date change something related to this, these AI reviews. We should likely define more what is okay in each state of this EIP. So what is okay for draft? What should be addressed in the review? What should be in Last Call? And that is a final. So that especially on the final state, this EIP, that we answer that we do not have to change anything about this. There's one URL I want to share. This is from the IETF and the RFC site. They are also studying RFC AI and large language models. It is a very nice discussion. Our post is a public chat, and it is worth it to read. So to give over, finally, what I want to do is to start AI reviews here as a pilot. And what we also want to do is, if an EIP or ERC changes the status from draft to review, we re-review the entire document to see if it matches the status, what we expect on these on the status. And we do not want to just any text influence the original identity of this EIP. So I think we should start to think about this, and of course this is harnessed: a human still skims the documents before approving, so we do not approve any slop or scam. Any questions or initial comments?
Sam: No, that's great. I think that aligns pretty closely with how I feel.

Pooja Ranjan: Yep. I have a couple of comments here. I mean, I'm generally in favor of AI review, or any way that can help editors to review these proposals, because we have too many proposals to review right now. But, uh, I am a little concerned of auto merging, especially at two statuses. One, when we are merging it at draft, and second, when we are merging it as final. Other than that, for review and last call, it seems fine and okay to be auto merged with AI review, but I feel like having human intervention at the level of draft and final would be useful. I love the idea of harnessing AI things more over time, yeah.

jochem-brouwer: Yes, okay. Not too clear on the presentation about this, but I do not want to automerge anything at all. The AI reviews, it is a read-only pilot. So this will send reviews, and then based on this, we still do a human check, if you can afterwards merge it or not. So I do not want to automate merging anything using AI. I just want to state this.
Pooja Ranjan: That is cool. I mean, at this stage, it sounds good to me. I wonder, yeah, if anyone has any question, comment, please feel free to unmute and share it.

jochem-brouwer: Maybe to address Marc's question. So Marc is asking, biggest EIP merge, is the initial review correct? And it is an interesting question, because I think I am starting to shift a little bit about this, because of the workflow. What we used to do in the past, which was before I was a formal editor, I would say, this idea of the lunch break, I will just review them, et cetera. But I realize these EIPs are actually going to get merged in the draft status. So directly, I think my work in the past was to always review the EIPs in the review status and not in the draft status. So what I think for the biggest EIP merge, the initial review is: what should be very clear before an EIP is in draft is that these ideas presented in the EIP, which will then get moved to be presented at ACD, is that this document is unambiguous. So it is very clear what the author intends to do with this EIP, and that it is self-contained. So doesn't… there is a certain quality of this EIP document. So it will be well-defined references, read it in one go. Because the idea is that if you read this document, we want to read it one go and not read it like two times in order to understand this. So in that sense, I would think that I can actually do a very good job about it still. We are not going to automate draft reviews. That will be automoted, but there is still human do into it. But I think the main realization is that the complexity of these, they are simply too complex at this point for me to initially crisply review. And this should not block the entire process. So if the draft looks okay, if it is understandable, then it is the job of like ACD and the ecosystem to figure out, okay, do you want this, do you want the change. That's of course the entire idea of the draft status. So yeah, I think this is here.
Justin Traglia: I have a question, and I might have just missed it from your presentation. When will the bot — or if and when will the bot — uh, re-review. Oh. Will it re-review?
jochem-brouwer: If an EIP, so whenever a PR, then the bot reviews it. And then the next review, I would say, the ones, uh, a new command, or if there have been comments added to this review.

jochem-brouwer: Yeah. You can also think about like the author explicitly adding and scan and ready. So maybe it waits two hours, and then if the bot reviews, then we send a review, and if not, then it reviews in two hours.

Justin Traglia: Okay, that's fair.

I do not want to do that.

jochem-brouwer: Yes, um. Okay. So look at this. These are mostly update EIP PRs. And I think this is also most likely related to this. This is a bad thing, but it is something to realize because taking the execution spec perspective, what we are seeing here is that we are seeing a lot of external EIP PRs being open. Because the finish you can, the sponsor, I like, okay, at this idea EIP implemented and upgrade this EIP PR. And this is also what is happening to EIPs. So, for instance, EIP-8037, I'm not going to check this, but I think that a lot of draft changes to EIP-8037 do not have anybody's policy on the editor side to close these, to guide us. Because I think currently this is not a responsibility. And because this is really on the side of the authors of these EIPs, like you, EIP editor, state, you merge, or you state that you do not want it closed. But that is likely also the wish. We have so many of these open PRs. But these design update EIP PRs, the people who open these PRs are not authors of these EIPs. So this will not get auto-merged.

I wonder if anyone else has any comment on this one? Yes.

jochem-brouwer: Yeah, maybe on this, the PR limit question. Like I think the problem of limiting the amount of PRs open by a new contributor, is that if you have ideas, if you are a new contributor and just specific ideas about many EIPs, for instance Hegota EIPs, present state, okay, you can only open three PRs. This is not the way how we should gate-keep IDs. It is not the right move for the EIPs repository slash ecosystem. Because the special, what sets it apart, is it is an open ecosystem. We have to figure another way to deal with this. But I think, I think maybe a good way to frame this is you should see each EIP as its own repository. And the EIPs repo is then like the monorepo of all these EIPs. So if you are an owner of an EIP, you have an external PR being open against it. The PR is open against, you have against repository of the. So yeah, I don't think the principle that to sort of date keeping.

jochem-brouwer: Because we are just going to add this thing. At some point this of course going to be like a very evolving document. Dhanush | EIPsInsight: GMGM, everyone. Thank you for having me. So I'll just share my screen first. So for those who might not be familiar with EIPsInsight, it's a platform where we track proposals through every stage, for network upgrades and the protocol calls behind them. We provide toolings and help measure editorial and contributor activity. So, yeah, as Pooja mentioned, one of the things we have been working on is EIP Builder. Uh, with the recent discussion around agents.md and AI-assisted EIP authoring, I thought that, uh, it would be a good opportunity to showcase what we already have, and how it could be useful to contributors and editors. Uh, I'll just, uh, so let me walk you through what, uh, we have built here. Let's collapse this. So this is the general UI of the EIP builder. Uh, so in general, uh, if you see there's different views, uh, where for the EIP builder, we have, uh, split screen, we have edit, mark and review, and another preview view. So, uh, in general, contributors can start a new EIP, fill in the required metadata, work through individual sections, and see the generated markdown here alongside the draft. And the EIP builder will handle the document structure, allowing authors to focus on the actual proposal. But yeah, beyond drafting a new EIP, we also have a built-in validation engine which uses the template from EIP-1 and in general EIP template and also eipw lint.

Dhanush | EIPsInsight: Uh, so, uh, yeah, let's start with a clean example. Uh, I'll just take an ERC, for example, import ERC, and I'll type 8113. I'll just press enter, and it will import the, uh, proposal MD file. We can see everything is here, and I'll just drag this on here. So, I'll, uh, just go on and try to validate it. It'll go, it'll check all the related rules. For example, this is how the validation works, how it generates errors, warnings, and suggestions, and it also follows RFC 2119. So, since this has already passed all the tests, I'll take another example of an older EIP, which might not follow the rule. So I'll just add, check in the EIPs and then I'll type the 1559 proposal. So yeah, uh, this is fairly an older proposal, and I'll just try to validate it once. And yeah, it shows that the description is missing. So it highlights all the section where changes is required or how critical is the change. For example, this is just a warning. This description missing thingy is one of the critical thingy. And also there is a specification validated. There is a few more warnings. Title should have been title case, to-do marker, and RFC 2119. Let's take another example. We'll take another ERC, which is 5114, I'll just change this to ERC, and I'll type 5114. So yeah, we'll just try to validate this too. And yeah, it specifically mentions RFC 2119 keywords are used, but the boilerplate paragraph is missing. So we'll just go to this particular section, which is specification. And we do get this specific button to insert RFC 2119 notice if it's not available there in the specification. So if I just press on it, the template would be appended in the specification section. So if you try to validate it again, yeah, so all checks have been passed and it's ready for submission. So yeah, but apart from this, we have another, we have built a dedicated PR review workflow too. So, for example, I choose a PR, for example, 12449. So it's an EIP, so I'll just choose EIP and I'll just type it again. 12449. So it brings in the proposal EIP-7773, which is the main proposal which has been changed in PR 12449. And it will show it's an open PR and it's ready for author. We'll just try to validate this too. And yep, it shows there's another warning according to like field scope security consideration. So it'll just highlight it. It'll give an advisory that it should not be none. So yeah, you can import an existing GitHub PR, inspect the proposal and run the same validation directly within the builder.

Dhanush | EIPsInsight: This makes it useful not just for contributors drafting new proposals, but also for editors reviewing existing ones. So yeah, what we are trying to do is we simply want to make it easier for more people to participate and arrive with better prepared proposals. Uh, yeah, I would love to hear your thoughts, if there are any additional features you'd like to see. And yeah, we'd like to make that first step easier and help more people participate in the EIP process. That's from my side, thanks. Happy to take any questions or suggestions, if anyone has any.
